note: Verification receipts for src/lib/profiles.ts. Every notableQuote is traced to a primary source; every rejected misattribution is recorded so it is never reintroduced.

quoteSources.quote: It is remarkable how much long-term advantage people like us have gotten by trying to be consistently not stupid, instead of trying to be very intelligent.
quoteSources.source: Letter to Wesco Financial shareholders, dated March 5, 1990, published in the Wesco Financial Corporation 1989 Annual Report. This is the earliest documented appearance of the line, confirmed by Quote Investigator.

quoteSources.quote: Show me the incentive and I will show you the outcome.
quoteSources.source: A signature Munger maxim repeated at Berkshire Hathaway and Daily Journal annual meetings. His fullest treatment of incentive-caused bias is the talk The Psychology of Human Misjudgment, collected in Poor Charlie's Almanack (2005). Wording is stable across citations, though Munger stated it conversationally rather than in a single canonical text.

quoteSources.quote: The big money is not in the buying and the selling, but in the waiting.
quoteSources.source: Poor Charlie's Almanack: The Wit and Wisdom of Charles T. Munger, edited by Peter D. Kaufman (2005).

quoteSources.quote: A great business at a fair price is superior to a fair business at a great price.
quoteSources.source: Poor Charlie's Almanack (2005). This is the principle Buffett repeatedly credits Munger with teaching him, moving Berkshire beyond Benjamin Graham style bargain hunting.

quoteSources.quote: The safest way to try to get what you want is to try to deserve what you want.
quoteSources.source: USC Law School commencement address, May 13, 2007, where it is the opening idea of the speech. Also appears in Poor Charlie's Almanack (2005). Some transcripts render it as 'try and get' and 'try and deserve'; the sense is identical.

quoteSources.quote: I constantly see people rise in life who were not the smartest, sometimes not even the most diligent, but they are learning machines.
quoteSources.source: USC Law School commencement address, May 13, 2007, immediately preceding his line that such people go to bed every night a little wiser than when they got up.

excludedMisattributions: 'To the man with only a hammer, every problem looks like a nail.' Munger cited this constantly and it is central to his case for multidisciplinary thinking, but it is a pre-existing proverb, known in psychology as Maslow's law of the instrument (1966). Excluded because it is not original to Munger.

'Invert, always invert.' Munger made inversion famous as a thinking tool, but he explicitly credited it to the nineteenth century mathematician Carl Gustav Jacob Jacobi. Excluded as a quotation of Munger's own.

'It's not supposed to be easy. Anyone who finds it easy is stupid.' Almost certainly said by Munger, but the circulating version traces to Howard Marks recounting a private conversation rather than to any Munger transcript, letter, or book, so the exact wording and context cannot be verified against a primary source.

'Spend each day trying to be a little wiser than you were when you woke up.' A polished paraphrase widely sold on posters. The documented 2007 USC wording is that learning machines go to bed every night a little wiser than when they got up. Excluded in favor of the verifiable sentence about learning machines.

'The world is not driven by greed, it's driven by envy.' Circulates in several incompatible wordings. Munger's verifiable framing, from the 2007 USC address, is that envy, resentment, revenge, and self-pity are disastrous modes of thought. Excluded because no single wording of the greed and envy version can be pinned to a primary source.

'Take a simple idea and take it seriously.' Genuinely Munger's, but the primary text in Poor Charlie's Almanack presents it as a two part rule, to take a simple, basic idea and then take it very seriously. Left out of the quote list because the popular one line form is a compression rather than his exact sentence.

'All I want to know is where I'm going to die, so I'll never go there.' Frequently posted as a Munger original. He used it as a joke to illustrate inversion, and it is his retelling of a folk formulation rather than a line he coined.

quoteSources.quote: But this is Day 1 for the Internet and, if we execute well, for Amazon.com.
quoteSources.source: Jeff Bezos, 1997 Letter to Shareholders, Amazon.com, Inc., published with the 1997 annual report and reprinted at https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/amazons-original-1997-letter-to-shareholders. Verified verbatim against Amazon's own reprint.

quoteSources.quote: We will continue to make investment decisions in light of long-term market leadership considerations rather than short-term profitability considerations or short-term Wall Street reactions.
quoteSources.source: Jeff Bezos, 1997 Letter to Shareholders, Amazon.com, Inc., first bullet of the section headed "It's All About the Long Term." Verified verbatim against Amazon's reprint at https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/amazons-original-1997-letter-to-shareholders.

quoteSources.quote: Day 2 is stasis. Followed by irrelevance. Followed by excruciating, painful decline. Followed by death. And that is why it is always Day 1.
quoteSources.source: Jeff Bezos, 2016 Letter to Shareholders, Amazon.com, Inc., released April 2017 (https://www.aboutamazon.com/news/company-news/2016-letter-to-shareholders). Verified verbatim; the two sentences are consecutive in the letter's opening section.

quoteSources.quote: I believe we are the best place in the world to fail (we have plenty of practice!), and failure and invention are inseparable twins.
quoteSources.source: Jeff Bezos, 2015 Letter to Shareholders, Amazon.com, Inc., released April 2016 (https://s2.q4cdn.com/299287126/files/doc_financials/annual/2015-Letter-to-Shareholders.PDF); the same passage is quoted in Ryan Mac, "Jeff Bezos Calls Amazon 'Best Place In The World To Fail' In Shareholder Letter," Forbes, April 5, 2016.

quoteSources.quote: I knew that if I failed I wouldn't regret that, but I knew the one thing I might regret is not ever having tried.
quoteSources.source: Jeff Bezos, interview with the Academy of Achievement, San Antonio, Texas, May 4, 2001 (https://achievement.org/achiever/jeffrey-p-bezos/), describing the regret minimization framework he used when deciding to leave D. E. Shaw. He restated the same idea in the 2010 Princeton Baccalaureate address.

quoteSources.quote: Cleverness is a gift, kindness is a choice.
quoteSources.source: Jeff Bezos, "We Are What We Choose," Baccalaureate address to the Princeton University Class of 2010, May 30, 2010 (https://www.princeton.edu/news/2010/05/30/2010-baccalaureate-remarks). Verified verbatim against Princeton's published text.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Your margin is my opportunity.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Excluded. The Quote Investigator study of this line traces its earliest appearance to Adam Lashinsky's November 2012 Fortune profile, "Amazon's Jeff Bezos: The Ultimate Disrupter," where it is characterized as "a favorite Bezos aphorism" rather than quoted from Bezos in the first person. No shareholder letter, speech, interview transcript or filing has been found in which Bezos says it. It may be a journalist's paraphrase of Amazon's pricing posture, so it fails the primary source test.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Your brand is what other people say about you when you're not in the room.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Excluded. Circulates on quote aggregator sites with no primary citation. The closest documented Bezos line, "A brand for a company is like a reputation for a person," is attributed to a 2004 BusinessWeek online interview with Robert D. Hof, but the original interview text could not be retrieved and verified, so both were left out.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Work hard, have fun, make history.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Excluded. This is an Amazon corporate slogan that appears on internal posters and recruiting material. It is routinely presented as a Bezos quotation, but no letter, speech or interview in his own words could be found as its origin.

excludedMisattributions.quote: We are stubborn on vision. We are flexible on details.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Excluded. Widely cited, usually to an unspecified shareholder letter or to a Wired interview, but the exact wording could not be confirmed against any primary text. Bezos has expressed the idea in interviews in looser form, so the crisp aphoristic version appears to be a compression by others.

excludedMisattributions.quote: If you double the number of experiments you do per year, you're going to double your inventiveness.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Excluded from the quote list. Bezos has made this argument repeatedly and a close variant appears in Amazon's 2015 shareholder letter discussion of experimentation, but this exact popular phrasing could not be matched verbatim to a primary source, so the verified 2015 letter sentence on failure and invention was used instead.

quoteSources.quote: Either you are running for food, or you are running from becoming food. And oftentimes, you can't tell which. Either way, run.
quoteSources.source: Commencement address, National Taiwan University, 26 May 2023. Transcript excerpts published by NVIDIA (https://blogs.nvidia.com/blog/2023/05/26/huang-ntu-commencement/). Delivered immediately after the better known line from the same speech, 'Run. Don't walk.' Punctuation normalized from the published semicolon; wording unchanged.

quoteSources.quote: For all of you Stanford students, I wish upon you ample doses of pain and suffering.
quoteSources.source: View From The Top interview, Stanford Graduate School of Business, 1 March 2024. Quoted verbatim in Fortune's report on the session (https://fortune.com/article/jensen-huang-advice-high-expectations-make-it-hard-to-succeed/) and in CNBC's coverage of 15 March 2024.

quoteSources.quote: Greatness comes from character, and character isn't formed out of smart people. It's formed out of people who suffered.
quoteSources.source: View From The Top interview, Stanford Graduate School of Business, 1 March 2024, as quoted by Fortune. The published transcript renders the second clause after a dash; a period is substituted here with no change to the words.

quoteSources.quote: Your pain and suffering will strengthen your character, your resilience and agility, and they are the ultimate superpowers.
quoteSources.source: Keynote address, Caltech 130th Annual Commencement, 14 June 2024. Present in the full published transcript of the address and in Caltech's own coverage of the ceremony.

quoteSources.quote: Our company is thirty days from going out of business.
quoteSources.source: Huang's standing opener for internal Nvidia presentations, dating to the near bankruptcy of 1996 and 1997. Documented in Tae Kim, The Nvidia Way (2024), and confirmed on the record by Huang, who said in a 2025 interview on The Joe Rogan Experience that he had used the phrase for thirty three years.

quoteSources.quote: Building a company and building Nvidia turned out to have been a million times harder than I expected it to be.
quoteSources.source: Interview on the Acquired podcast, episode 'NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang', October 2023 (https://www.acquired.fm/episodes/jensen-huang). Said in answer to whether he would found the company again, to which his immediate reply was 'I wouldn't do it.'

excludedMisattributions.quote: AI won't replace humans, but humans with AI will replace humans without AI.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Not Huang's line. The aphorism traces to Harvard Business School professor Karim Lakhani. Huang has said a distinct version of the idea, 'You're not going to lose your job to an AI, but you're going to lose your job to someone who uses AI,' at the Milken Institute Global Conference on 6 May 2025, but the Lakhani formulation is routinely reposted under Huang's name and was excluded.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Don't learn to code.
excludedMisattributions.reason: A three word clip that inverts the argument. At the World Governments Summit in Dubai in February 2024 Huang said it is the industry's job to build computers that nobody has to program, that 'everybody in the world is now a programmer,' and that students should therefore go deep on domains such as biology, chemistry and finance. Excluded as a distortion rather than a quote.

excludedMisattributions.quote: I'd rather torture my employees into greatness than fire them.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Paraphrase, not verbatim. In a fireside conversation with Patrick Collison at Stripe Sessions in May 2024 Huang said, 'I'd rather torture you into greatness because I believe in you,' speaking in the second person about coaching rather than about employees as a class. The circulated third person version was excluded.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Nvidia GPUs power Ethereum and Solana, and this crypto mass adoption event will double your holdings.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Entirely fabricated. Taken from an AI generated deepfake livestream impersonating an official Nvidia GTC keynote, which drew roughly 95,000 concurrent viewers before YouTube removed it and which directed viewers to a QR code crypto doubling scam. No such statement was ever made.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Stay hungry, stay foolish.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Not Huang. The line comes from the final issue of the Whole Earth Catalog and was popularized by Steve Jobs in his 2005 Stanford commencement address. It circulates on quote aggregator sites under Huang's name alongside other unsourced hustle aphorisms, all of which were excluded for lacking any primary source.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Purported Huang predictions of specific Nvidia share prices or market capitalization targets.
excludedMisattributions.reason: No such statement appears in his keynotes, earnings calls or on the record interviews; he does not give share price guidance. These typically originate in investment promotion content and were excluded. Relatedly, all valuation and net worth figures in this profile carry explicit as of dates because they move daily.

quoteSources.quote: Seek wealth, not money or status. Wealth is having assets that earn while you sleep. Money is how we transfer time and wealth. Status is your place in the social hierarchy.
quoteSources.source: Opening post of the How to Get Rich (Without Getting Lucky) thread, May 31, 2018 (x.com/naval/status/1002103360646823936); reprinted verbatim in The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (2020), p. 30.

quoteSources.quote: You will get rich by giving society what it wants but does not yet know how to get. At scale.
quoteSources.source: How to Get Rich (Without Getting Lucky) thread, May 31, 2018; reprinted verbatim in The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (2020), p. 30.

quoteSources.quote: Pick an industry where you can play long-term games with long-term people.
quoteSources.source: How to Get Rich (Without Getting Lucky) thread, May 31, 2018; reprinted verbatim in The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (2020), p. 31, and the title of the chapter Play Long-Term Games with Long-Term People.

quoteSources.quote: Specific knowledge is knowledge you cannot be trained for. If society can train you, it can train someone else and replace you.
quoteSources.source: How to Get Rich (Without Getting Lucky) thread, May 31, 2018; reprinted verbatim in The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (2020), p. 32.

quoteSources.quote: Escape competition through authenticity.
quoteSources.source: A standalone Naval tweet, identified as such by Ravikant himself in The Almanack of Naval Ravikant (2020), p. 43, where he says it was a tweet that did not go into the How to Get Rich tweetstorm.

quoteSources.quote: A fit body, a calm mind, a house full of love. These things cannot be bought - they must be earned.
quoteSources.source: Naval tweet, February 2018 (x.com/naval/status/966512979066765313). He calls it his favourite tweet and unpacks it in his own essay A Calm Mind, a Fit Body, a House Full of Love (nav.al/finally-wealthy, May 21, 2019).

excludedMisattributions.text: Give me a lever long enough and a place to stand, and I will move the earth.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Archimedes, not Ravikant. He quoted it inside the How to Get Rich thread and the Almanack prints it with an explicit Archimedes attribution (p. 33), but it circulates widely on quote pages as a Naval original.

excludedMisattributions.text: Play stupid games, win stupid prizes.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Appears in the Almanack as a line of Ravikant's, but the proverb long predates him. Variants of win stupid prizes are in print by the early 1990s and the phrase spread as an internet image macro from roughly 2012. Not original to him, so excluded.

excludedMisattributions.text: To find a worthy mate, be worthy of a worthy mate.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Charlie Munger, quoted by Ravikant in the Almanack with attribution to Munger. Frequently reposted under Ravikant's name.

excludedMisattributions.text: Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Apocryphal, usually pinned on Albert Einstein with no documented source. It attaches to Ravikant because of his compounding posts, but he did not write it.

excludedMisattributions.text: Happiness is a state where nothing is missing.
excludedMisattributions.reason: A compressed paraphrase, not a verbatim quote. What Ravikant actually wrote is: Happiness is what's there when you remove the sense that something is missing in your life (Almanack, Learning Happiness). The short version is excluded as unverifiable in that wording.

excludedMisattributions.text: A calm mind, a fit body, and a house full of love. These things cannot be bought. They must be earned.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Reordered. The Almanack prints this word order, but the original February 2018 tweet reads A fit body, a calm mind, a house full of love. The tweet wording is used above instead.

excludedMisattributions.text: Unsourced aphorisms circulated by Naval-quote fan accounts and quote-aggregation sites
excludedMisattributions.reason: General exclusion. Large volumes of generic self-improvement lines are published under his name with no tweet, essay, podcast or Almanack page behind them. Nothing was included here that could not be traced to his own posts, his own essays, an on-record appearance, or the Almanack's free full text.

excludedMisattributions.text: Spouse and marriage details
excludedMisattributions.reason: Not a quote, but excluded on the same standard. Ravikant refers to his wife in the Almanack, yet no reliable source names her; the circulating name comes only from low-quality celebrity-biography sites. The spouses field is therefore omitted, as is net worth, for which no well-documented figure exists.

quoteSources.quote: Every moment in business happens only once. The next Bill Gates will not build an operating system. The next Larry Page or Sergey Brin won't make a search engine. And the next Mark Zuckerberg won't create a social network. If you are copying these guys, you aren't learning from them.
quoteSources.source: Peter Thiel with Blake Masters, Zero to One (Crown Business, 2014), p. 1. Cited to that page on Wikiquote.

quoteSources.quote: What important truth do very few people agree with you on?
quoteSources.source: Peter Thiel with Blake Masters, Zero to One (Crown Business, 2014), p. 5. The same question appears verbatim in Blake Masters' notes on CS183 Class 1, Stanford, Spring 2012.

quoteSources.quote: All happy companies are different: each one earns a monopoly by solving a unique problem. All failed companies are the same: they failed to escape competition.
quoteSources.source: Peter Thiel with Blake Masters, Zero to One (Crown Business, 2014), chapter 3, "All Happy Companies Are Different." Thiel presents it as an inversion of the opening line of Tolstoy's Anna Karenina.

quoteSources.quote: Monopoly is the condition of every successful business.
quoteSources.source: Peter Thiel, "Competition Is for Losers," The Wall Street Journal, September 12, 2014, an essay adapted from Zero to One; the same claim runs through chapter 3 of the book.

quoteSources.quote: Brilliant thinking is rare, but courage is in even shorter supply than genius.
quoteSources.source: Peter Thiel with Blake Masters, Zero to One (Crown Business, 2014). Thiel restated and expanded the point in a 2015 Independent Institute talk.

quoteSources.quote: We wanted flying cars, instead we got 140 characters.
quoteSources.source: Tagline of the Founders Fund manifesto "What Happened to the Future?" (2011). Wikiquote records Thiel delivering the line himself in his 2014 talk at Yale.

excludedMisattributions: "Madness is rare in individuals, but in groups, parties, nations and ages it is the rule." Friedrich Nietzsche, Beyond Good and Evil, aphorism 156. Thiel quotes it approvingly in Zero to One, so quote sites frequently credit it to him. It is not his line.

"All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way." Leo Tolstoy, Anna Karenina. Thiel builds his monopoly maxim by inverting it, and aggregators often attribute the Tolstoy half to Thiel. Only the inverted business sentence is his.

"Don't fuck up the culture." Widely repeated as Thiel's advice to Airbnb after Founders Fund invested in 2012, but it is attested only secondhand, through Brian Chesky's April 2014 Medium post recounting the meeting. No on-record Thiel statement of it exists, so it is not presented as a quotation.
"Show me the incentive and I will show you the outcome." Charlie Munger. It appears on several quote aggregators under Thiel's name. Not his.

"Competition is for losers, and monopolies are for winners." A distorted mashup circulating on social media. The sourced lines are the WSJ headline "Competition Is for Losers" (September 12, 2014) and, separately, "Monopoly is the condition of every successful business." The compound sentence is not something he wrote.
"The Singularity is near." Ray Kurzweil, whose work Thiel has discussed and funded adjacent research to. Not a Thiel quotation.

Facebook stake figures: the 2004 investment is frequently rounded to "10 percent" or inflated to later valuations. The documented terms are $500,000 in August 2004 for 10.2 percent, structured as a convertible note tied to a 1.5 million user milestone that Facebook narrowly missed and that Thiel converted anyway.

PayPal founding framing: PayPal is often described as founded by Thiel and Elon Musk together in 1998. Thiel cofounded Confinity in December 1998 with Max Levchin, Luke Nosek, and Ken Howery; Musk's separate company X.com merged with Confinity in March 2000, and the merged entity was renamed PayPal in June 2001.

Palantir founding date and sole-founder framing: Palantir was founded in 2003 by Thiel with Alex Karp, Joe Lonsdale, Stephen Cohen, and Nathan Gettings. Karp, not Thiel, has been CEO since 2004; Thiel is chairman. Claims that Thiel founded it alone, or dates of 2004 or 2005, are inaccurate.

Thiel Fellowship amount: the figure is often quoted as a flat "$100,000" without qualification. That was the grant at the 2010 launch, paid over two years; the amount has since been increased, and the age ceiling has moved from under 20 to 22 or younger.

Gawker litigation motive: many secondary accounts assign Thiel specific motives for funding the Bollea suit. Only the verifiable record is stated here, namely the funding amount reported by Forbes in May 2016, the March 2016 verdict, the June 2016 bankruptcy, and the November 2016 settlement.

Net worth: trackers disagree sharply, with figures from roughly $12 billion to $28 billion in 2026. Only the Forbes figure and its as-of date are stated, with the New York Times December 2025 estimate given for comparison.

Children: several low-quality aggregator sites give specific ages and details for Thiel's children. Wikipedia's infobox lists none. The field is left deliberately hedged rather than repeating unsourced particulars about minors.

quoteSources.quote: There is only one boss. The customer. And he can fire everybody in the company from the chairman on down, simply by spending his money somewhere else.
quoteSources.source: Sam Walton with John Huey, Sam Walton: Made in America, My Story (Doubleday, 1992). Cited to that book under Sam Walton in Oxford Essential Quotations (Oxford University Press), which is the strongest scholarly attribution available; no page number is given there.

quoteSources.quote: The secret of successful retailing is to give your customers what they want.
quoteSources.source: Sam Walton: Made in America, My Story, p. 221 in the Bantam paperback edition. Walton introduces it as the one guiding principle he stuck to for his whole career in retail.

quoteSources.quote: Every time Wal-Mart spends one dollar foolishly, it comes right out of our customers' pockets.
quoteSources.source: Sam Walton: Made in America, My Story, chapter 1, p. 13.

quoteSources.quote: If I had to single out one element in my life that has made a difference for me, it would be a passion to compete.
quoteSources.source: Sam Walton: Made in America, My Story, foreword, p. xiii.

quoteSources.quote: I have always been driven to buck the system, to innovate, to take things beyond where they've been.
quoteSources.source: Sam Walton: Made in America, My Story, p. 61. Exact substring of the full sentence, which reads: 'for some reason in business, I have always been driven to buck the system, to innovate, to take things beyond where they've been.'

quoteSources.quote: Swim upstream. Go the other way. Ignore the conventional wisdom. If everybody else is doing it one way, there's a good chance you can find your niche by going in exactly the opposite direction.
quoteSources.source: Rule 10 of Sam Walton's Ten Rules for Building a Business, set out in Sam Walton: Made in America, My Story and reproduced verbatim by Walmart at corporate.walmart.com/about/sam-walton/10-rules-for-building-a-better-business.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Capital isn't scarce; vision is.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Everywhere online under Walton's name, but it traces only to a 2004 quotation anthology (Leslie Pockell, The 101 Greatest Business Principles of All Time) and downstream quote aggregators. No text in Made in America, none of the Ten Rules, and no documented Walton speech or interview supports it. Excluded.

excludedMisattributions.quote: High expectations are the key to everything.
excludedMisattributions.reason: One of the most reproduced Walton lines on quote sites, with no primary source anywhere. The nearest thing he actually wrote is in Made in America, chapter 2: 'I've always held the bar pretty high for myself: I've set extremely high personal goals.' Excluded in favour of sourced material.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Outstanding leaders go out of their way to boost the self-esteem of their personnel. If people believe in themselves, it's amazing what they can accomplish.
excludedMisattributions.reason: A staple of leadership training decks, but attributed to Walton only through the same 2004 quotation anthology and the aggregators that copied it. It appears neither in Made in America nor in the Ten Rules. Excluded.

excludedMisattributions.quote: I pay low wages. I can take advantage of that. We're going to be successful, but the basis is a very low-wage, low-benefit model of employment.
excludedMisattributions.reason: The only quotation Wikiquote lists for Walton, yet its earliest traceable appearance is a Wired column by Adam L. Penenberg published April 21, 2005, thirteen years after Walton's death, with no contemporaneous transcript, interview, or document behind it. Excluded as unverifiable in either direction.

excludedMisattributions.quote: The first Walmart opened in Bentonville, Arkansas.
excludedMisattributions.reason: A recurring factual misattribution rather than a quotation. Bentonville is where Walton's 5 & 10 variety store opened in 1950 and where Walmart's headquarters sits. The first Walmart, branded Wal-Mart Discount City, opened at 719 West Walnut Street in Rogers, Arkansas, on July 2, 1962.

quoteSources.quote: Your work is going to fill a large part of your life, and the only way to be truly satisfied is to do what you believe is great work. And the only way to do great work is to love what you do.
quoteSources.source: Stanford University commencement address, June 12, 2005. Official Stanford transcript and video; also carried verbatim in the sourced section of Wikiquote.

quoteSources.quote: Your time is limited, so don't waste it living someone else's life.
quoteSources.source: Stanford University commencement address, June 12, 2005. Quoted here as the opening clause only; the full sentence continues about not being trapped by dogma.

quoteSources.quote: It's not just what it looks like and feels like. Design is how it works.
quoteSources.source: Interview with Rob Walker for "The Guts of a New Machine," The New York Times Magazine, November 30, 2003. Full passage begins "Most people make the mistake of thinking design is what it looks like."

quoteSources.quote: A lot of times, people don't know what they want until you show it to them.
quoteSources.source: BusinessWeek interview, May 25, 1998. Listed in the sourced section of Wikiquote with that citation.

quoteSources.quote: Focusing is about saying no.
quoteSources.source: Closing question-and-answer session at Apple's Worldwide Developers Conference, May 1997. On video and in published transcripts of the session, in the context of cancelling OpenDoc.

quoteSources.quote: Being the richest man in the cemetery doesn't matter to me ... Going to bed at night saying we've done something wonderful ... that's what matters to me.
quoteSources.source: The Wall Street Journal, 1993. Ellipses reproduce the elisions in the published citation. Note that the cemetery figure of speech long predates Jobs and was used by the comedian Ed Wynn in the 1930s; Jobs is the source of this sentence, not of the image.

excludedMisattributions: "Stay hungry. Stay foolish." Jobs really did say this, as the last line of the 2005 Stanford address, but it is not his. He states in the speech itself that it was the farewell message on the back cover of the final issue of Stewart Brand's Whole Earth Catalog, the 1974 Whole Earth Epilog. Excluded because presenting it as a Jobs aphorism reverses the credit he was careful to give.

"Here's to the crazy ones. The misfits. The rebels ... the ones who do." This is advertising copy for Apple's 1997 Think Different campaign, written at TBWA\Chiat\Day by copywriter Rob Siltanen with Ken Segall, from a concept by art director Craig Tanimoto under Lee Clow. Jobs approved it and recorded a narration that Apple did not air, but he did not write it. Excluded as agency copy, not a Jobs statement.

"Good artists copy; great artists steal." Jobs did say this on camera in the PBS documentary Triumph of the Nerds (1996), but he explicitly attributed it to Picasso. The Picasso attribution is itself unverified and the sentiment traces to T. S. Eliot's 1920 essay on Philip Massinger. Excluded because it is a quotation of a quotation of doubtful origin.

"Innovation distinguishes between a leader and a follower." One of the most reproduced Jobs lines on the internet and it has no primary source. It circulates only through quote aggregators and secondary business books such as Carmine Gallo's The Innovation Secrets of Steve Jobs (2010). No interview, speech, keynote or published transcript containing it has been located. Excluded.

"I want to put a ding in the universe." Widely attributed and widely used, but it circulates in at least two incompatible wordings, ding and dent, with no agreed date, publication or transcript behind either. Excluded pending a citable primary source.

"Simplicity is the ultimate sophistication." Used in Apple's 1977 Apple II brochure and therefore associated with Jobs, but it is an aphorism attributed to Leonardo da Vinci and predates him by centuries. Excluded.
"The musicians play their instruments. I play the orchestra." Line of dialogue written for the 2013 feature film Jobs. There is no record of Jobs saying it. Excluded.

The viral deathbed essay beginning "I reached the pinnacle of success in the business world" and continuing that wealth is meaningless. A hoax. It first surfaced online in November 2015, more than four years after his death, was never published by any outlet with access to Jobs, and has been debunked by Snopes and Truth or Fiction. His reported last words, per his sister Mona Simpson's eulogy in The New York Times of October 30, 2011, were "OH WOW. OH WOW. OH WOW." Excluded.

"Do you want to sell sugared water for the rest of your life, or do you want to come with me and change the world?" Almost certainly said in substance, but the only source is John Sculley's own memoir Odyssey: Pepsi to Apple (1987), that is, one participant's recollection of a private 1983 recruiting conversation, quoted from memory years later. Excluded from the quote list as secondhand and unverifiable, though it is retained in the record as a documented Sculley account.
"My girlfriend always laughs during sex, no matter what she's reading." Circulates on quote sites under Jobs's name. It is a joke by the comedian Emo Philips. Excluded.

REJECTED: 'It's not the gold diggers who get rich, it's the shovel sellers.' An old proverb repeated in profiles about him, not an original Armstrong line.

REJECTED as current: 'Coinbase's mission is to create an open financial system for the world.' Verbatim from the 2020 post and the 2021 S-1, and accurate only as of that period. Coinbase's stated mission today is to increase economic freedom in the world. The two must not be conflated, so this is described in the career and legacy text with its date rather than listed as a standing quote.

EXCLUDED from notableQuotes: 'I would like us to all in crypto think about how we actually go create physical places in the world to preserve freedom over the long term. I think that's ultimately crypto's destiny.' Reported by The New Republic as a line from a podcast interview. The wording is secondhand from a magazine quoting audio, so it does not meet this profile's primary-source bar for a verbatim quote.

EXCLUDED as unverifiable text: the 'Letter from our Co-Founder and CEO' in Coinbase's February 25, 2021 Form S-1 is filed as page images rather than machine-readable text in the EDGAR document, so no quotation was drawn from it. The S-1 is used only for facts stated in its text body.

FLAGGED as opinion, not fact: his podcast characterizations of specific officials and of the SEC acting unlawfully are his stated beliefs, partly relayed hearsay, not established findings. They are excluded from this profile entirely, and the regulatory section states only what was filed, when, and how it resolved.

EXCLUDED from figures: his on-air estimates that the legal fight cost 'maybe in the 50 to 100 million range' and depressed the stock by 'I don't know, 10, 20 billion maybe more'. Rough spoken recollections, not audited or independently verified.

CORRECTED from the podcast transcript: he recalls the $25 million round as Union Square Ventures and Ribbit with Andreessen Horowitz at Series B. The documented record is a roughly $5 million Series A led by Union Square Ventures in May 2013 and a $25 million Series B led by Andreessen Horowitz in December 2013 with Union Square Ventures and Ribbit Capital participating. This profile uses the documented version.

CLARIFIED on valuation: first-day Coinbase valuations were reported anywhere from about $65 billion to over $112 billion depending on the price point and share count used. This profile uses the $328.28 closing price and the roughly $85 billion figure reported at the close.

CLARIFIED on the founding date: Coinbase's SEC filings say inception in May 2012, while the company and most accounts date the founding to June 2012, when it launched publicly. Both are stated rather than one being silently chosen.

CORRECTED on the Giving Pledge: he signed it in 2018 as the first cryptocurrency entrepreneur to do so, but Bloomberg reported in July 2024 that he had been removed from the signatory list. He must not be described as a current signatory. Likewise GiveCrypto.org, launched in 2018, wound down in 2023 and must not be described as active.

CLARIFIED on net worth: trackers disagreed materially through 2026, with published estimates ranging from roughly $7.4 billion to $9.4 billion depending on the date and the source. This profile cites one source with one as-of date rather than averaging them.

CLARIFIED on Fairshake: Fairshake is an industry super political action committee funded by multiple companies and investors, not Armstrong's personal committee. Coinbase, the corporation, was among its largest donors. Descriptions of it as 'Armstrong's super PAC' are imprecise.

NOT INCLUDED: any assessment of Coinbase stock, cryptocurrency, or any asset as an investment. This profile contains no investment or financial advice and none should be inferred from the quotations, which describe his company's stated mission and thesis.

quoteSources.quote: I aim not to be clever, but to be dogged.
quoteSources.source: James Dyson, Against the Odds: An Autobiography (1997). His full sentence in the book is "As I have often said, I aim not to be clever, but to be dogged." Reproduced with that book attribution in David Senra's published reading notes on Against the Odds (world.hey.com/davidsenra) and by SUCCESS magazine's profile of Dyson. Dyson restated the line himself, unprompted, in his 2025 filmed conversation with Senra.

quoteSources.quote: There is no such thing as a quantum leap. There is only dogged persistence, and in the end you make it look like a quantum leap.
quoteSources.source: James Dyson, Against the Odds: An Autobiography (1997). Printed on Goodreads' quote page for the book as "There is no such thing as a quantum leap. There is only dogged persistence, and in the end you make it look like a quantum leap." The published text uses a dash before the final clause; it is rendered here as a comma to match house style, with no change of wording.

quoteSources.quote: I am claiming nothing but the virtues of a mule.
quoteSources.source: James Dyson, Against the Odds: An Autobiography (1997), from the passage "At any stage in my story where I talk of vision, and arrogance seems to have got the better of me, remember that I am celebrating only my stubbornness. I am claiming nothing but the virtues of a mule." Quoted with that book attribution in the Founders podcast episodes on the book and in published reading notes on it.

quoteSources.quote: Misfits are not born or made; they make themselves.
quoteSources.source: James Dyson, Against the Odds: An Autobiography (1997). Listed as a direct quotation from the book, alongside "I have been a misfit throughout my professional life, and that seems to have worked to my advantage", in getAbstract's summary of Against the Odds (citing the Thomson Texere edition, 2003) and in David Senra's published reading notes on the same book. Some quote sites file these lines under Invention: A Life; the sourced attributions point to Against the Odds, so that is the attribution used here.

quoteSources.quote: Invention is often more about endurance and patient observation than brainwaves.
quoteSources.source: James Dyson, Invention: A Life (2021), from the passage "Research is about conducting experiments, accepting and even enjoying failures, but going on and on, following a theory garnered from observing the science. Invention is often more about endurance and patient observation than brainwaves." Carried verbatim on Goodreads' quote page for the book.

quoteSources.quote: Failure is interesting. It's part of making progress. You never learn from success, but you do learn from failure.
quoteSources.source: James Dyson, interviewed by Nadia Goodman for Entrepreneur, November 2012, "James Dyson on Using Failure to Drive Success" (entrepreneur.com/growing-a-business/james-dyson-on-using-failure-to-drive-success/224855), also syndicated by NBC News. The article prints an em dash after "interesting"; it is rendered here as a period to match house style, with no change of wording.

excludedMisattributions.text: 5,127 prototypes over 15 years.
excludedMisattributions.reason: The most common Dyson myth, and a conflation of two separate spans. The 5,127 hand built prototypes are concentrated in the coach house years at Bathford, roughly 1979 into the early 1980s, ending with the Kleeneze Rotork Cyclon of 1983 and 1984 and then the G-Force in Japan in March 1986. The fourteen year arc in Against the Odds runs from tearing the bag off his Hoover at the age of thirty one to the first fully operational and visually perfect Dual Cyclone on 2 May 1992, his forty fifth birthday. Both are stated separately in this profile and never merged.

excludedMisattributions.text: He spent 15 years creating 5,126 versions that failed before he made one that worked.
excludedMisattributions.reason: The framing used in Entrepreneur's own 2012 article and repeated by many aggregators. The interview quotation from that article is used here, but its surrounding arithmetic is not, since it merges the two spans and revises the prototype count.

excludedMisattributions.text: After five years and about 5,127 prototypes, Dyson launched the G-Force cleaner in 1983.
excludedMisattributions.reason: A compressed sentence in the English Wikipedia article on James Dyson that runs two products together. The machine sold in 1983 and 1984 was the Kleeneze Rotork Cyclon, roughly 500 units; the G-Force was a reworked version put into production in Japan by Apex in March 1986. The company article on Wikipedia states the corrected sequence, which is what this profile follows.

excludedMisattributions.text: A clever person doesn't spend 14 years building 5,127 prototypes of the world's first cyclonic vacuum cleaner. A determined person does.
excludedMisattributions.reason: David Senra's own line, written while reading the books and stated as such in the Founders episode. It is not a Dyson quotation and circulates as one.

excludedMisattributions.text: Difference and retention of total control.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Senra's one line compression of Dyson's philosophy. Dyson's own phrasings are difference for the sake of it and retain total control, so the compound slogan is not quoted as his.

excludedMisattributions.text: Successes teach you nothing. Failures teach you everything. Making mistakes is the most important thing you can do.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Circulates widely on quote aggregator sites with no primary citation traceable to a book, interview or speech. The sourced Entrepreneur line about never learning from success is used instead.

excludedMisattributions.text: I made 5,127 prototypes and there were 5,126 failures.
excludedMisattributions.reason: The prototype count is his and is documented, but this exact sentence is an aggregator construction. No quoted form of the number is used anywhere in this profile.

excludedMisattributions.text: You never change things by fighting the existing reality. To change something, build a new model that makes the existing model obsolete.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Buckminster Fuller, whom Dyson admires and quotes. Frequently reposted under Dyson's name.

excludedMisattributions.text: If you ask people what they want, they want a faster horse.
excludedMisattributions.reason: An apocryphal Henry Ford line, raised in conversation around Dyson's dismissal of market research. Not Dyson's, and not Ford's on any documented record.

excludedMisattributions.text: Excellence is the capacity to take pain, and the hard way is the right way.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Senra's maxims, used while narrating Dyson's story, the second credited by him to Jerry Seinfeld. Not Dyson's words.

excludedMisattributions.text: His father was forty when he died.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Not a quote, but excluded on the same standard. Sources disagree on Alec Dyson's age at death, giving both forty and forty three, so no age is stated. What is consistently documented is that he died of cancer in 1956, when James was nine, and that the school allowed James to remain.

excludedMisattributions.text: Motor speed figures of 130,000 or 140,000 rpm, and the Dyson Institute salary quoted in dollars.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Dyson cites motor speeds conversationally with varying numbers, and published Institute salary figures are in pounds and have changed over time. No rpm figure and no salary number is asserted in this profile, only that Institute students are paid and pay no tuition fees.

quoteSources.source: inRegister Magazine (Baton Rouge), 'Todd Graves, Founder and CEO, Raising Cane's Chicken Fingers,' published April 30, 2013, where it appears as his own line in a first person profile. quoteSources.quote: When you're an entrepreneur and you believe in something to your core, you use every no and every 'it's not going to work' as fuel.
quoteSources.source: Chase Withorn, Forbes, September 24, 2025, in the profile of Graves as America's richest restaurateur, quoted in the passage about being turned down by every bank he approached.

quoteSources.quote: If you try to be all things to all people, you won't be special.
quoteSources.source: Chase Withorn, Forbes, September 24, 2025, quoted in the passage on why the menu has never expanded. Verified by fetching the article.

quoteSources.quote: I profited $30 my first month, and I was thrilled.
quoteSources.source: Entrepreneur, 'How to Develop the Mindset for a Billion-Dollar Success, According to Raising Cane's Founder,' July 29, 2025, from his on the record interview on The Playbook. Independently corroborated by other outlets that report the thirty dollar first month profit.

quoteSources.quote: There is not a balance of life at a startup. You have to put 100% into it.
quoteSources.source: Entrepreneur, July 29, 2025, same interview, on what the first years actually cost. Consistent with his CNBC Make It remarks of November 4, 2024 about working fifteen and sixteen hour days in a row.

excludedMisattributions.quote: His professor gave the Raising Cane's business plan a failing grade.
excludedMisattributions.reason: The most repeated version of the founding story and it is wrong. Graves has said on the record that the grade was a B minus, the lowest in the class, and that the instructor's problem was the single item concept rather than the plan itself. The F grade version appears in aggregator write ups and headlines with no primary source. Excluded, and the B minus is used in the prose.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Todd Graves is an LSU graduate.

excludedMisattributions.quote: The distracted don't beat the focused.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Spoken by podcast host David Senra in a 2025 Founders episode about Graves, who only agreed with it. It is the host's framing, not a Graves quote, and it is excluded along with everything else in that machine generated transcript that is not clearly in his own voice.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Money comes naturally as a result of service.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Attributed by David Senra to Henry Ford during the same episode. Graves' own version of the thought is that if you do things for the right reasons in business the money will come, so the idea is paraphrased in prose and the Ford line is not quoted as his.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Praise costs nothing and means everything.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Speaker attribution is ambiguous in the auto generated podcast transcript, where Graves' recorded reply is only an agreement. Excluded rather than quoted as his.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Raising Cane's has never franchised, ever.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Overstated. Graves did sell franchises in a handful of markets early on and later bought them back, a small number of franchised restaurants remain in the United States, and all international restaurants operate through franchise partners. The accurate claim is that he stopped selling domestic franchises and bought back the ones he had sold, which is how the prose puts it.

excludedMisattributions.reason: Startup funding figures diverge across reputable outlets. Forbes reports roughly $50,000 of his own savings, $90,000 from investors and a $50,000 SBA loan; other 2024 reporting gives $50,000 of savings, about $100,000 from friends and family, and an SBA loan. Because the sources conflict, the prose names the three sources of capital and states plainly that published accounts differ on the amounts.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Raising Cane's employs 75,000 crew members and the business is worth more than $20 billion.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Both figures come from Graves speaking on a podcast and neither is independently documented for a private company. Published sources put the crew count around 65,000 to 70,000 for 2025, and the only well sourced valuation style number is the Forbes estimate of his personal fortune. The company debt figure quoted in the same conversation is likewise undocumented and excluded.

excludedMisattributions.quote: He is worth $11.5 billion.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Not false so much as stale and method dependent. Wealth trackers have diverged sharply on Graves because Raising Cane's is private: Bloomberg published a figure near $11.5 billion in April 2025 while Forbes had him at $22 billion in July 2026. The profile uses the Forbes number, attributes it to Forbes, and gives the as of date rather than stating a flat valuation.

excludedMisattributions.quote: The 1,000th Raising Cane's opened on March 18, 2026.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Sources disagree by a day: some coverage ties March 18, 2026 to the preview and celebration event and other coverage gives March 19, 2026 as the public opening. The profile says March 2026 rather than pick a contested day.

excludedMisattributions.quote: Graves appeared on ABC's Secret Millionaire in 2011.
excludedMisattributions.reason: He appeared on the Fox version of Secret Millionaire, in the premiere episode, reported by Nation's Restaurant News on December 1, 2008 ahead of its December 3, 2008 air date. ABC revived the format later, which is the source of the mixed up network and year in some write ups.

quoteSources.quote: Mild success can be explainable by skills and labor. Wild success is attributable to variance.
quoteSources.source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Fooled by Randomness: The Hidden Role of Chance in Life and in the Markets (2001). Verified two ways. Open Library full text search inside the scanned trade edition returns Fooled by Randomness as a matching book for the phrase "Wild success is attributable to variance", so the sentence is in the book itself and not only on quotation sites. The WIST quotation database independently cites it to Fooled by Randomness, Part 1, Chapter 1, page 12, with a link to the corresponding Internet Archive page image.

quoteSources.quote: Missing a train is only painful if you run after it!
quoteSources.source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Black Swan: The Impact of the Highly Improbable (2007). Open Library full text search inside the scanned trade editions returns The Black Swan under Taleb's name, in more than one edition and in the Incerto four book bundle, as containing the phrase "Missing a train is only painful if you run after it". In the book it follows Taleb's account of the advice "I don't run for trains", which he credits to his friend Jean-Olivier Tedesco, and it is immediately extended to not matching the idea of success that others expect of you. The exclamation mark is as printed.

quoteSources.quote: The three most harmful addictions are heroin, carbohydrates, and a monthly salary.
quoteSources.source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Bed of Procrustes: Philosophical and Practical Aphorisms (2010). Open Library full text search inside the scanned trade edition returns The Bed of Procrustes as a matching book for the phrase "heroin, carbohydrates, and a monthly salary", confirming the aphorism is in the book. The Week also printed it with that book attribution in its collection of aphorisms drawn from The Bed of Procrustes.

quoteSources.quote: Wind extinguishes a candle and energizes fire.
quoteSources.source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder (Random House, 2012), the opening sentence of the Prologue, section I, headed HOW TO LOVE THE WIND. Read directly in the publisher's typeset prologue that Taleb hosts on his own site at fooledbyrandomness.com/prologue.pdf, so this is the book text rather than an aggregator. In the book the sentence continues into the instruction to use randomness, uncertainty and chaos rather than hide from them.

quoteSources.quote: If you see fraud and do not say fraud, you are a fraud.
quoteSources.source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Antifragile: Things That Gain from Disorder (Random House, 2012), Prologue, where it is introduced by the words "First ethical rule". Read directly in the publisher's typeset prologue on Taleb's own site at fooledbyrandomness.com/prologue.pdf. This line is very widely cited to Skin in the Game; that attribution is wrong, and the correction is confirmed here against the Antifragile text itself.

quoteSources.quote: Never cross a river if it is on average four feet deep.
quoteSources.source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, Skin in the Game: Hidden Asymmetries in Daily Life (2018), where the rule appears in his treatment of ruin, sequence and non ergodicity. The sentence was verified in Taleb's own signed essay The Logic of Risk Taking, published by him on Medium's Incerto publication on 25 August 2017, which prints it as "never cross a river if it is on average four feet deep" alongside "in order to succeed, you must first survive"; that essay is Incerto material that was carried into the book. The initial capital here is house style for a standalone sentence, with no change of wording. Note that Skin in the Game is not in the Open Library scanned corpus, so the phrase could not be checked against a scan of the book itself; the author's own published essay is the traceable source used.

excludedMisattributions.text: "Don't tell me what you think, tell me what you have in your portfolio."
excludedMisattributions.reason: HELD BACK, NOT USED. Almost certainly genuine and almost certainly from Skin in the Game, where it accompanies his account of refusing to comment on Microsoft stock on television because he was neither long nor short it. But Skin in the Game is not in the Open Library scanned corpus, so it could not be checked against the book text, and every source found for it was a book summary blog, a quote site or Goodreads. Under the standard applied here that is not enough, so it was left out of the quotation list rather than presented as verified.

excludedMisattributions.text: "Antifragility is beyond resilience or robustness."
excludedMisattributions.reason: VERIFIED BUT NOT SELECTED. Confirmed directly in the Antifragile prologue on Taleb's own site, immediately after he coins the word. Dropped only so that the six quotations span all five Incerto volumes instead of taking three from Antifragile. Available if a replacement quote is ever needed.

excludedMisattributions.text: "What doesn't kill me makes me stronger."
excludedMisattributions.reason: Nietzsche, from Twilight of the Idols. Constantly presented as a Taleb line or as a one sentence summary of antifragility. Taleb discusses and complicates it in Antifragile; he did not write it.

excludedMisattributions.text: "We suffer more often in imagination than in reality."
excludedMisattributions.reason: Seneca, quoted by Taleb in Antifragile. Routinely reattributed to Taleb by quotation aggregators. Taleb quotes the ancients constantly and credits them, which is exactly why lines he merely cites get laundered into lines he wrote.

excludedMisattributions.text: "Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence."
excludedMisattributions.reason: Not original to Taleb. The formulation long predates him and is popularly associated with Carl Sagan and Martin Rees. Taleb uses it in The Black Swan as an inherited maxim, so it is not presented as his.

excludedMisattributions.text: "The market can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent."
excludedMisattributions.reason: Attributed to Keynes, itself on thin evidence, and not Taleb's. Filed under his name on several quote sites because of the subject matter.

excludedMisattributions.text: "The stock market is a device for transferring money from the impatient to the patient."
excludedMisattributions.reason: Warren Buffett. Not Taleb's, and not in any Incerto volume.

excludedMisattributions.text: Any inspirational, TED style aphorism in the register of "enrich lives" circulating under Taleb's name.
excludedMisattributions.reason: Taleb publicly denounced a fabricated quotation attributed to him on X in March 2019, stating that he never uses phrasing of that kind and calling it a fake quote. Every circulating aphorism in that register was therefore treated as suspect and excluded.

excludedMisattributions.text: "You will never fully convince someone that he is wrong; only reality can."
excludedMisattributions.reason: SOURCE UNSETTLED. Better sourced references place it in Skin in the Game while several aggregators file it under The Bed of Procrustes, and Open Library full text search returned no match at all, which is inconclusive rather than disconfirming since Skin in the Game is not in that scanned corpus. Because the volume cannot be named with confidence, and every quotation here must carry a named volume, it was excluded.

excludedMisattributions.text: "Not everything that happens happens for a reason, but everything that survives survives for a reason."
excludedMisattributions.reason: Commonly attributed to Antifragile. The exact wording could not be confirmed against the book text, only against aggregators, so it was left out.

excludedMisattributions.text: Taleb coined the term black swan.
excludedMisattributions.reason: He did not. The black swan as a figure for the supposedly impossible traces to the Roman satirist Juvenal and was a standing European expression. Taleb repurposed it for rare, high impact, retrospectively rationalised events, and says so himself. The legacy section states it as a repurposing, not an invention.

excludedMisattributions.text: Nassim Nicholas Taleb is Distinguished Professor of Risk Engineering at NYU Tandon.
excludedMisattributions.reason: TITLE CORRECTED. Most profiles, including Wikipedia, still use the present tense. NYU Tandon's own faculty page now lists him as Retired Distinguished Professor in the Department of Finance and Risk Engineering, verified on the university page in July 2026. The profile states the September 2008 appointment and the current retired title separately.

excludedMisattributions.text: Taleb runs, manages or trades for the hedge fund Universa Investments.
excludedMisattributions.reason: ROLE CLARIFIED. He is Distinguished Scientific Advisor to Universa and describes the involvement as deliberately passive. Mark Spitznagel, his former Empirica partner, is Universa's founder and chief investment officer. Claims that Taleb runs a hedge fund today are wrong.

excludedMisattributions.text: Empirica's fund returned 56.86% in 2000; Universa returned 65% to 115% in October 2008, or roughly 4,000% in the first quarter of 2020.
excludedMisattributions.reason: EXCLUDED FROM THE PROFILE. These figures are reported secondhand, are not audited public numbers, and in the Universa cases Taleb did not manage the capital. They are not presented as his personal results.

excludedMisattributions.text: Spouse and children.
excludedMisattributions.reason: OMITTED. Wikipedia's article body mentions a 1988 marriage and two children. Taleb is markedly private about his family, the detail is thinly cited, and no primary or infobox confirmation was found, so under the standard of omitting anything not well documented both fields were left out rather than asserted.

excludedMisattributions.text: Net worth.
excludedMisattributions.reason: OMITTED. No credible published figure exists. Taleb has said he became financially independent after Black Monday in 1987, which is stated in the career section, but the circulating net worth numbers trace to celebrity finance sites with no methodology and were not used.

excludedMisattributions.text: METHOD NOTE.
excludedMisattributions.reason: BrainyQuote, AZQuotes, QuoteFancy, QuotePark, Quote Catalog, Bookey, thecitesite and user submitted Goodreads pages were treated only as leads to be checked, never as sources. Goodreads states plainly that its quotations are community added and unverified. Every quotation in this profile was confirmed either by reading the publisher's typeset text on Taleb's own site, by full text search inside the scanned trade edition of the named book, or in Taleb's own signed essay.

quoteSources.quote: Pain + Reflection = Progress.
quoteSources.source: Principles: Life and Work (2017), Life Principles. Published verbatim by Dalio at https://www.principles.com/principles/4a903526-2db6-4a0a-9b71-889868f0f475/ under the heading 'Pain + Reflection = Progress.'

quoteSources.quote: The two biggest barriers to good decision making are your ego and your blind spots.
quoteSources.source: Principles: Life and Work (2017), Life Principle 'Recognize your two barriers,' under 'Be Radically Open-Minded.' Published verbatim by Dalio at https://www.principles.com/principles/a46a8d1b-7bc8-420c-92ec-903f30b4be36/ and repeated in his own posts on LinkedIn and X.

quoteSources.quote: Rather than thinking, 'I'm right,' I started to ask myself, 'How do I know I'm right?'
quoteSources.source: Ray Dalio, TED2017 talk 'How to build a company where the best ideas win,' April 2017, describing the aftermath of his 1982 depression call. Present in the talk transcript and corroborated in TED's own session report at https://blog.ted.com/the-human-response-the-talks-of-session-3-of-ted2017/

quoteSources.quote: I gained a humility that I needed in order to balance my audacity.
quoteSources.source: Ray Dalio, TED2017 talk 'How to build a company where the best ideas win,' April 2017, spoken in the same passage about 1982. Present in the talk transcript; TED's session report carries the same line in slightly compressed form.

quoteSources.quote: If you're not failing, you're not pushing your limits, and if you're not pushing your limits, you're not maximizing your potential.
quoteSources.source: Principles: Life and Work (2017), Life Principles, in the passage on embracing failure. Published verbatim by Dalio at https://www.principles.com/principles/4a903526-2db6-4a0a-9b71-889868f0f475/

quoteSources.quote: Radical truth and radical transparency are fundamental to having a real idea meritocracy.
quoteSources.source: Principles: Life and Work (2017), Work Principle 'Trust in Radical Truth and Radical Transparency.' Published verbatim by Dalio at https://www.principles.com/principles/f6412dca-b3f9-4dd0-bb65-274869dd21ed and reposted by him on X.

excludedMisattributions: 'He who lives by the crystal ball will eat shattered glass,' and its variant ending 'is destined to eat ground glass.' Quotefancy, BrainyQuote, AZ Quotes and dozens of finance accounts credit this to Dalio. The line is an older Wall Street aphorism associated with the economist Edgar R. Fiedler (1929 to 2003), who is quoted with it as 'He who lives by the crystal ball soon learns to eat ground glass.' Dalio repeats it; he did not originate it. Excluded as a line he merely quotes from others.

'The economy is now flat, teetering on the brink of failure.' Widely reproduced as his 1982 congressional testimony, but every version traces back to secondary retellings rather than to a located transcript of the hearing. Excluded pending a primary source.

'Diversification is the Holy Grail of investing.' A compressed aggregator paraphrase. What Dalio actually argues is a longer and more specific claim about combining fifteen to twenty genuinely uncorrelated return streams. The one line version is not his sentence, and the underlying point is investment strategy rather than a life principle, so it is excluded on both grounds.

'Cash is trash.' Genuinely said by Dalio on CNBC at Davos on January 21, 2020, so it is not a misattribution, but it is time bound market commentary rather than a durable principle, it was followed within weeks by the COVID crash, and it would read as investment advice. Excluded deliberately.

'The quality of your life is determined by the quality of your decisions.' Circulated under Dalio's name on quote sites, but it is a generic self help formulation attached to many different authors with no primary Dalio source. Excluded.

Quotes sourced only to Goodreads, BrainyQuote, AZ Quotes, Quotefancy or similar aggregators were rejected as a class. Dalio is heavily quote farmed, and every line kept above traces to text he published himself at principles.com or to his own recorded TED2017 talk.
